narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. While the average accepted student ranks around the 6th decile, you placed in the 3rd decile, signaling weaker performance in later law school years. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction, each pulling the prediction toward success. Your LSAT of 35.5 is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, and your 3.5 undergraduate GPA is actually higher than the 3.23 average among those who were admitted. These academic strengths helped reduce the risk, but they were not enough to overcome the impact of your third-year ranking.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record in upper-year courses and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score further. Improving in these areas would most effectively increase your chances of admission in a future application cycle. (218 words)
